1. SCOPE
for the determination of colour of refined oils such as undyed motor and aviation gasoline, jet propulsion fuels, naphthas, and kerosine, and, in addition, petroleum waxes and pharmaceutical white oils. 2.

1.1 This method is intended

TERMINOLOGY

2.0 For the purpose of this method, the following definition shall apply. 2.1 Saybolt Colour -A number related to the depth of a column of material, the colour of which is compared with specified glass standards. The ra.tge of numbers is +30 (lightest colour) to -16 (darkest colour), '

APPARATUS

4.1 The Saybolt

chromometer, illustrated in Fig. 1, .consists of sample and standard tubes, optical system, light source, and colour standards. The different parts of the chromometer are described in 4.1.1 to 4.1.10.

4.1.1 Oil Sample Tube - For' testing liquids, use a No. 7740 Pyrex glass tube, or its equivalent in colour~characteristics (see Note l), having an inside diameter of not less than 16.5 mm nor more than 17.5 mm, and an outside diameter of not less than 21.25 mm nor more than 22.75 mm. Close the tube at the bottom with an optically clear plano glass disc 6.25 mm thick, free of striations and scratches. The tube shall be 508 to 516 mm long from the upper surface of the plano disc to the top ofthe tube. Mount the tube and disc in a suitable metal collar provided with a petcock to pctrmit controlled drainage of the tube (see Fig. 1). Construct the collar in a manner that permits removal of the glass disc for cleaning. Etch at intervals of cverv 25.4 mm a line completely around the tube starting at a point which will be 50.8 mm above the top surface of the plano disc when the tube is in the collar: number these lines consecutively 2 to 20 startling 2

4.1.6 Illuminction - Arrange for the light to be transmitted through the tubes by means of a reflectin mirror of either white opal glass or clear glass, with a uniform coating o ? untarnished silver on one surface. Fix the mirror at a suitable angle, and so arrange it that reflected light of equal intensity of radiation will pass through the tubes in parallel rays. Alternatively, diffused light may be projected directly up through the tubes from the base of the instrument. For the light source, use an artificial daynght lamp The diffused light shall be free of glare or shadows. Interfering light from all other sources shall be excluded.
SO arranged as to project a diffused light up through the tubes.

4.1.9 Lamp - Use a lamp bulb rated at 60 W. It shall -be constructed of clear glass, inside frost finish, and shall be rated at approximately 13 lumens per watt and 2 750" Kelvin colour temperature. Attach to a standard socket reflector, hemispherical in form (see Fig. l), the interior surface of which is finished with a brilliant aluminium bronze powder, free from mica and other adulterants, and applied with a wheat-resistant bronzing liquid sprayed uniformly over the surface. This finish shall be such as to be free from selective absorption, and have an initial +eflectiyity above 65 percent. 4.1.10 Duyli& Filter Glass (see Note 3) - concave-convex in form? and dust-tight. It shall fit closely over the opening in the hemispherical reflector (set Fig. 1). The glass filter shall be finished on its concave surface by sand-blasting and acid-smoothing oi fortifying. An acceptabk daylight filter shall possess such characteristics that the trilinear co-ordinates (x, y and z) and the luminous transmission I,,,, when calculated from the spectral transmission data using the 1931 ICI Standard Illuminant A, are as shown in Table II.
NATE 3 -A spectrophotometric test of an acceptable filter should indicate a transmission of radiant energy not less than 60 percent at 410 m,u, with a smooth curve down to a transmission below 10 percent at 700 rnp. This curve, furthermore, should not have the pronounced hump &at is characteristic of scccss cobalt. The typical cobalt curve has an increased transmission at a wavelength of 570 w above a straight line drawn behvem the points 540 and 590 my, and also a transmission band in the red for wavelengths of 600 and greater. 5. STANDARDIZATION 5.1 Remove

OF APPARATUS

the glass disc from the bottom of the oil sample tube. Clean When deposits are not removable the disc, oil sample tube, and plain tube. by wiping or sohent rinsing, wash with soap and water. After cleaning, rinse with distilled water and with acetone or some other suitable solvent, and dry. Assemble the oil sample tube, and position the tubes in the instrument. Using the specified light source and illumination, observe the comparative light intensity of the two-halves of the optical field, with both tubes empty, and with the 12-mm diaphragm removed from under the plain tube. The intensity of-light observed in each half of the optical field shall be the same. Ad.justment m the position of the light source may be necessary to Replace the 12-mm diaphragm under the plain tube, achieve this match. and fill the oil sample tube to the sample tube division 20 with distilled The intensity of the light observed in each half of the optical field water. shall be the same, for the instrument to be judged satisfactory for use. 6. PREPARATION OF SAMPLE of qualitative

6.1 If the material is turbid, filter through a sufficient number filter papers (Whatman No. 4 or equivalent) until it is clear.

6.2 When preparing paraffin wa-x for testing, do not heat excessively, because oxidation may occur with consequent discolouration of the sample. 7. PROCEDURE

8. PROCEDURE

FOR

PETROLEUM

WAX

8.1 Heat the wax sample to 8.5 to 17�C above its melting point. Preheat the oil sample tube. Pour the liquid wax into the oil sample tube; turn the heating clemcnts off, and, after the heat waves in the sample are no longer noticeable, obtain the required readings as directed in 7. 9.
